title: Judge orders Kinew government to disclose who excluded Tesla from Manitoba EV rebate program and why
summary: A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric-vehicle…

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric-vehicle rebate program — and explain why that decision was made.
'Exceptional and unusual' step taken by judge following 'baffling coyness' from provincial government

A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric vehicle rebate program — and explain why that decision was made.

In an order issued Nov. 13, Court of King's Bench Justice Elissa Neville gave Wab Kinew's government 10 days to produce "a complete record" of the decision-making process that disqualified anyone who purchased Tesla vehicles after March 19, 2025, from qualifying for Manitoba's EV rebates.
This means the NDP government has until Monday to explain the decision, which Tesla initially asked the court to overturn in May.

For the past six months, Tesla has argued the decision was unreasonable, untransparent and unfair because, the company contends, it's not clear who actually decided to exclude Tesla from the EV rebate program and whether that person was legally authorized to make that decision.
The government, in turn, has argued the exclusion can not be reviewed in court because it was a funding decision.

items: Tesla asks court to overturn exclusion from Manitoba EV rebate program

blocks.text: In her order, Neville said she can not make any determination without knowing who made the decision and said the NDP government has displayed "a baffling coyness" about the decision-making process.

"The disputed record filed with the court sheds no light whatsoever on the question of who made the Tesla exclusion decisions, how they made the decisions, why they made the decisions, and whether these decisions are reviewable," Neville wrote.
"The respondents' position, in effect, appears to be that the reviewability of the decision must be determined before they can identify the decision maker and produce the record."
The judge went on to note it is not routine for courts to order governments to disclose the rationale behind decisions.
"I acknowledge that compelling the respondents to file their record by way of an affidavit is an exceptional and unusual remedy," Neville wrote.

"That said, in the specific and unique circumstances of this case, where the respondents refuse to identify anyone as the decision maker, such an approach strikes me as the more practical and efficient means of ensuring that there is a clear and streamlined record before the court."
Rebates yanked on budget day 2025

Manitoba's EV rebate rolled out in 2024 but was retroactive to 2023. It entitled Manitobans buying a new electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid priced below $70,000 to a $4,000 rebate. Used and leased EVs qualified for a $2,500 or $1,000 rebate, respectively.

On provincial budget day in 2025, Finance Minister Adrien Sala said removing Tesla from the EV rebate was about "Trump-proofing our economy" and a "commitment to be elbows up." Chinese EVs were also excluded at the time.
Manitoba Finance Minister Adrien Sala speaks to reporters on March 20, 2025, when he unveiled a provincial budget that excluded Tesla from EV rebates. (Jaison Empson/CBC)
Tesla argued this exclusion ran counter to the stated purpose of the EV rebate program and also cost consumers $560,000.

items: Tesla's exclusion from Manitoba EV program 'incredibly unfair,' politically motivated, court hears

blocks.text: During a court hearing in October, Tesla's legal counsel noted Premier Wab Kinew said in 2025 that Tesla CEO Elon Musk should "get Donald Trump to stop the tariffs, and then we can talk about the EV rebate."

In her order, Justice Neville voted "in the absence of a proper record, the applicant says it has only media reports and public remarks from Manitoba's Premier through which to glean the rationale for the Tesla exclusion decision.
The province, she noted, considered the EV rebate change to be a policy decision made under the government's spending power.

"The applicant is entitled to seek to challenge a decision affecting its interests. The respondents intend to argue in this case that the decision the applicant challenges is not reviewable because it is a policy decision," she wrote.

"I cannot make that determination without knowing who the decision-maker was. For some reason, the respondents are saying that it is for the court to make that determination, even though the respondents have neither taken a position nor provided the information necessary for me to do so."
A motion by the government to strike the Tesla application will be heard at the same time as the application, Neville said.
Tesla's Winnipeg legal counsel declined further comment.
The NDP government declined comment as well.

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation.
